opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's because the talk itself is kind of deceptively simple. On the surface, Yann has been saying roughly the same things for years: the cake analogy, self-supervised learning as the bulk of the cake, world models, the limits of autoregressive LLMs, energy-based models, JEPA. If you hear it once, you might think, okay, I get it. But every time I hear it again, I'm in a different place in my own research, so different parts of it hit differently.

When I was a PhD student, I mostly heard the slogans. Later, after I'd actually worked on representation learning, on things like contrastive learning and masked autoencoders, I started to understand *why* he frames things the way he does. For example, his point that you shouldn't predict every pixel and should predict in representation space instead. The first time, that sounded like a philosophical preference. Then you train these models yourself, you see where the capacity goes, you see what the representations actually learn, and you realize it's a very concrete technical claim with real consequences.

The other thing is that Yann thinks on a very long time horizon. A lot of what he says isn't meant to be immediately actionable. It's more like a map of where the field should be in ten years. So the talk works almost like a compass. Whenever the field gets overly excited about one direction, like scaling a particular architecture, I go back to his framing and ask: does this actually get us closer to a system that understands the physical world, that can plan, that has persistent memory, that can reason? That question stays useful even if you don't agree with every specific answer he gives.

And to be fair, I don't agree with everything. Some of his claims are deliberately provocative. But that's also part of the value. A strong, consistent position gives you something to push against. Even when I disagree, I have to articulate *why*, and that sharpens my own thinking.

So it's not that the slides change much. I change. Each time I come back with new experience and new confusion, and the same talk answers a different question.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses limits of autoregressive LLMs and questions overinvestment in particular architectures; it does not say LeCun’s ideas are compatible with today’s dominant modeling paradigm.

r004.rationale: The candidate presents the talk as a compass for questioning whether research focused on one direction advances longer-term goals, suggesting it can help redirect research beyond a narrow focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's because the talk isn't really a talk about results. It's a talk about a worldview. Most research talks you hear once, you get the method, you get the numbers, and you're done. Yann's talk, the one about autonomous machine intelligence, JEPA, world models, all of that, it's more like a map of what he thinks intelligence requires, and he's been refining that map for years.

So every time I hear it, I'm a different person. When I first heard it, I was mostly working on vision architectures, ConvNeXt and things like that, and I probably nodded along at the parts about self-supervised learning and skipped over the rest. Then I started caring about generative models and video, and suddenly the part where he argues against predicting pixels directly, the argument for predicting in representation space, that hit me completely differently. I remember thinking, oh, he's been saying this the whole time and I just wasn't ready to hear it.

That's the thing about it. It's layered. There's the engineering layer, there's the cognitive science layer, the stuff about how babies learn intuitive physics, and there's this almost philosophical layer about what a model should and shouldn't be forced to do. You only absorb the layer that matches whatever problem is bothering you at the moment.

And frankly, the field keeps changing around the talk too. When LLMs got huge, a lot of people thought his skepticism about autoregressive models was just contrarianism. Then you watch the field hit real walls on reasoning, on planning, on sample efficiency, and you go back to the same slides and they read like a diagnosis rather than a complaint.

So I don't think I'm finding new things in the talk, exactly. I think the talk is stable and I keep moving, and each time the distance between where I am and where he's pointing tells me something about what I should work on next. That's a pretty rare property for a research talk to have.

r001.rationale: The speaker says the talk lands differently as their own work and interests change, and that they were not ready to absorb some ideas earlier. This attributes deeper understanding to their experience, not repetition alone.

r002.rationale: The response describes LeCun’s skepticism about autoregressive models and says the field has hit walls; it does not say his ideas are compatible with today’s dominant modeling paradigm.

r003.rationale: The response discusses layered ideas and changing research concerns, but does not explain how translating the ideas into shared conceptual language connects them to concrete work being done today.

r004.rationale: The response says the talk can suggest what to work on next, but does not suggest that LeCun’s ideas could move current AI research beyond a local optimum.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because I’m listening with a different set of questions each time. The talk may be similar, but after working on a problem and running into difficulties, I’ll hear something and think, “Oh, that’s what he meant.” Something that sounded abstract before suddenly feels very concrete.

Yann also tends to talk about the bigger picture—what we’re trying to achieve and what’s missing from our current approaches. You can understand the words the first time without really appreciating the implications. As your own experience grows, you find another layer in the same idea. So it’s not necessarily that he’s saying something new every time; it’s that I’m able to hear something new.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because the talk stays the same, but my understanding changes. The first time I hear an idea, I might understand the words without really appreciating the problem behind it. Then I spend time doing research, run into difficulties, and listen again. Suddenly, something he said feels very concrete: “Oh, that’s what he meant.”

So each time, I’m connecting his ideas to a different set of experiences. It doesn’t mean I agree with everything. But I find myself understanding more of the reasoning behind his perspective, and that gives me something new to think about.
